title: Galactic Quartet
caption: The galaxy quartet NGC 6845, imaged by the Gemini South telescope
celestial: NGC 6845 · constellation Telescopium · about 270 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/G. Gimeno, R. J. Díaz, H. Dottori. Image processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Four interacting galaxies share this view from Gemini South, all of them caught up in each other's gravity. The pair at the top are well-defined spiral galaxies, while the two below them are disk-shaped lenticular galaxies. Together they are known as NGC 6845, roughly 270 million light-years from Earth.

They sit in the constellation Telescopium, fittingly, one of a handful of constellations that honor scientific instruments instead of animals or figures from mythology. Between the galaxies are signs of star-forming regions and filaments of stars that have been pulled away from the galaxies they started in.

Because they are relatively close neighbors, the galaxies are interacting, and their mutual gravity is subtly distorting them. Astronomers believe the two spirals will eventually evolve into lenticular galaxies. A lenticular galaxy is a disk galaxy without prominent spiral arms, often with little ongoing star formation.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (5.48 x 4.84 arcminutes) and distance (270 million light years), the frame spans roughly 430,000 × 380,000 light-years. Its light set out about 270 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Taken with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph on Gemini South through r, i and z filters. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The z filter reaches into near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and the long exposure gathers far more light than the eye.
